title: What Happens During Air Duct Cleaning?
h1: What Happens During a Professional Air Duct Cleaning?
description: Here's what a proper air duct cleaning looks like from start to finish: inspection, negative pressure, agitation, register cleaning and a final check.
quick_answer: A proper duct cleaning starts with an inspection, then the technician connects a powerful vacuum to put the duct system under negative pressure. Brushes, air whips or compressed air knock debris loose so it's pulled into the vacuum instead of your rooms. Registers, the return and the blower area get cleaned too, and the system is checked before the crew leaves.
body:
What happens before the cleaning starts?

A good crew begins by looking around. The technician finds the furnace or air handler, which in most San Diego and Orange County homes sits in the attic, garage or a hall closet. They count supply registers and returns, check the filter, and look at the condition of the ducts where they can see them.

This is also when they'll point out problems that cleaning alone won't fix, like crushed or disconnected flex duct in the attic, signs of rodents, or mold on the coil. Floors near registers get covered, and the system is shut off at the thermostat.

How do they actually clean the ducts?

The key idea is negative pressure. The ductwork is put under suction so loosened dust goes into the collection equipment instead of floating into your rooms.

  1. Seal the registers. Supply vents are covered so the vacuum pulls from the right place.
  2. Connect the vacuum. A high-powered vacuum, either truck-mounted or a portable HEPA-filtered unit, is attached to the main trunk or plenum.
  3. Agitate the debris. Working one branch at a time, the technician feeds rotary brushes, air whips or skipper balls into the duct. These knock dust and debris off the duct walls.
  4. Pull it out. The vacuum draws the loosened material down the duct and out of the house.
  5. Clean the returns. Return ducts often collect the most dust because they pull unfiltered house air. They get the same treatment.
  6. Clean registers and grilles. Covers are removed, washed or wiped, and reinstalled.

Do they clean the furnace and coil too?

They should, at least the parts that are part of the air path. Cleaning the ducts but leaving a dusty blower wheel or a dirty plenum means the clean ducts get dirty again quickly. Depending on the job, the technician may vacuum the blower compartment, clean the return plenum and look at the evaporator coil.

Ask what's included before the work starts. A cheap "whole house" special that only vacuums the registers isn't the same service.

What about sanitizing and sealing?

These are optional add-ons, not part of every cleaning.

  • Sanitizing applies an EPA-registered product inside the ducts after cleaning. It's most useful after rodent activity, water damage or a musty odor problem.
  • Duct sealing and repair fixes gaps, loose connections and torn flex duct. Leaky attic ducts pull in dust and hot attic air, so sealing them helps cleaning results last longer.

A technician should only recommend these when there's a reason, and should be able to show you what they found.

What should it look like when they're done?

Before leaving, the crew should reinstall all registers, put in a fresh filter if you have one ready, turn the system back on and confirm air is flowing at each vent. Ask to see before-and-after photos or video of a few duct runs. A careful crew takes them as a matter of course, and they show you the work was actually done.

How long does it take, and how should I prepare?

Most single-story homes take a few hours. Larger homes, two-story houses with more than one system, or ducts with heavy debris take longer. The technician can give you a better idea once they've counted registers and looked at the system.

To help the day go smoothly:

  • Clear a path to the furnace or air handler, including any boxes stored in front of a garage unit or hall closet.
  • Make sure the attic hatch is reachable if the equipment or ducts are up there.
  • Move small furniture and fragile items away from registers and return grilles.
  • Keep pets in a closed room, since doors will be opening and equipment hoses run through the house.
  • Have a new filter on hand in the right size.

Signs your ducts are due for cleaning

  • Dust blowing out of registers when the system kicks on
  • Visible debris or pet hair inside return grilles
  • Recent remodeling, drywall work or a move into a home that sat empty
  • Rodents in the attic or crawl space
  • A musty smell when the heat or AC runs
  • Heavy wildfire smoke exposure

If any of those sound familiar, our air duct cleaning team can inspect your system and give you a free estimate. You can also check current specials before you book.
faqs: It shouldn't be. Because the ducts are kept under negative pressure, loosened dust gets pulled into the vacuum instead of into your rooms. The crew should cover floors near the work area and clean up before leaving.
Do I need to be home during duct cleaning?
Someone should be there to let the crew in, show them where the equipment is and walk through the results at the end. You don't need to watch the whole job.
Can I use my heat or AC right after duct cleaning?
Yes. Once the registers are back on and the system has been tested, it's ready to use. Put in a clean filter so you're not pulling old dust back into the system.
How often should air ducts be cleaned?
There isn't one schedule that fits every home. Many homeowners clean every few years, sooner after remodeling, rodent problems, water damage or heavy smoke exposure.
